What should a seller expect from Detroit, Michigan?

Detroit anchors Wayne County as its seat and ranks first in Michigan by population. French explorers founded Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit here in 1701, and by 1920 the auto industry had lifted it to fourth place among American cities. The population then fell from its 1950 peak of 1.85 million, the city filed for bankruptcy in 2013 and left it in 2014, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate of 649,095 residents sits above the 639,111 counted in 2020.

A seller here deals with 138.7 square miles of land, according to the Census. A house in Boston-Edison or Indian Village competes in a different market from a modest bungalow elsewhere in the city, even though both pay the same city and county taxes. The county records the deed and holds older delinquent tax accounts, so many sale questions end at a county office.

How does the Detroit housing market compare in Census numbers?

Detroit has the lowest home values and the fewest owner-occupants of the four Michigan cities profiled in this batch of pages. Close to half of Detroit households rent, so investors and landlords are a real part of the buyer pool.

A typical owned home at $83,900 beside a typical rent of $1,074 means a rented house can repay its price quickly, which is why investors follow Detroit sales. The same gap makes a roof or furnace replacement a much heavier share of a sale price here than in Dearborn, where the typical owned home is $218,800.

What kinds of houses and neighborhoods do Detroit sellers have?

Beyond downtown and New Center, Detroit is mostly low-rise. Working-class areas built before World War II have wood-frame and brick houses, while Brush Park, Woodbridge, Indian Village, Palmer Woods and Boston-Edison have larger, more ornate homes. Forty-two significant structures are on the federal historic register, and the Guardian Building became a National Historic Landmark in 1989.

The ground is flat. The city slopes gently from northwest to southeast over glacial and lake clay, with the Detroit Moraine, a broad clay ridge about 62 feet above the river, under the older districts. Weather and soil shape what an inspector flags:

  • Temperatures stay at or below freezing on roughly 44 days a year, so furnaces, roofs and plumbing get attention.
  • About 12 days a year top 90 degrees, which puts cooling and attic ventilation on the checklist.
  • Clay under older blocks makes basement moisture and drainage fair questions.

Fix these items or price them in before you list.

Which employers, schools and transit options help Detroit buyers?

Midtown's Detroit Medical Center employs more people than anyone else in the city, with Wayne State University beside it and the Henry Ford Health System in New Center. General Motors, Rocket Mortgage, Ally Financial and DTE Energy keep headquarters here, and roughly 80,500 people work downtown, one-fifth of the city's jobs. Buyers who work in those districts look for housing nearby.

The river adds a draw of its own. The Detroit River International Wildlife Refuge covers islands, wetlands and shoreline along 48 miles of the Detroit River and western Lake Erie, and the city's attractions bring about 16 million visitors a year. Downtown redevelopment around Campus Martius Park, Grand Circus Park, Ford Field, Comerica Park and Little Caesars Arena adds to the pull.

The Detroit Public Schools district is the largest in Michigan, and charter schools enroll a large additional group. Many families also look at suburban districts, so ask your agent how school boundaries affect the buyer pool on your street.

Getting around is easier than in many Michigan cities. DDOT buses, the QLINE streetcar and the downtown People Mover loop serve the core, and SMART runs routes to the suburbs. Detroit has four crossings to Windsor, Ontario, the newest being the Gordie Howe International Bridge, which opened in 2026.

What state taxes and fees apply when a Detroit house sells?

Michigan puts its deed tax on the seller. Every $500 block of value carries $3.75 of state tax, and a county layer sits on top: 55 cents per block in a county under two million residents. MCL 207.523, 207.525 and 207.504 set the framework, and the Wayne County deed office confirms the current county rate. You have 15 days from handing over the deed to pay the county treasurer.

MCL 207.526 exempts certain deeds, including a court-ordered transfer with no stated price, a foreclosure deed, and an instrument that creates a joint tenancy where one of the owners already held the property. A lender that later resells a foreclosed house does not get the same break.

  • The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor inside 45 days (MCL 211.27a).
  • For the next calendar year, taxable value is set at the SEV.
  • Ask the Detroit assessor for the form that ends your own principal residence exemption.

For current-year and past-due bill amounts, ask the City of Detroit Office of the Assessor and the Wayne County Treasurer for written payoff figures before you sign anything.

Why does tax foreclosure timing matter for Detroit sellers?

The Wayne County Treasurer, whose office is at 400 Monroe Street in Detroit, holds an annual online auction of tax-foreclosed properties. The minimum bid is a fixed amount that includes the treasurer's foreclosure and auction costs, winners have 72 hours to pay in full, and the office records a quit claim deed within 30 days after the auction closes.

Selling before the auction lets you choose the buyer and the price. Ask the treasurer what redemption rights remain on your parcel and whether a payment plan is available. Have the closing agent settle any balance from your proceeds, since a buyer's lender expects the lien cleared when the deed changes hands.

How do you compare offers on a Detroit house that needs work?

Three questions decide most Detroit sales: what an appraiser will accept, what an inspector will list, and what taxes are still open on the parcel. A mortgage buyer needs all three to line up. An investor offer skips the appraisal, and an as-is contract can say who clears trash, personal property and open utility accounts.

Line up offers by what you walk away with: price, minus deed tax, minus unpaid taxes and liens, minus repairs you would otherwise fund. Ask each bidder for evidence of funds and a dated closing plan before you choose.

More questions about Detroit, MI

Which side owes the state deed tax on a Detroit house?

The seller. Michigan names the grantor as the liable party. The state takes $3.75 on each $500 block, Wayne County adds its portion, and a court-ordered transfer without a stated price is among the exempt deeds.

Can a Detroit house with unpaid taxes still be sold?

Yes. Request an official payoff letter from the Wayne County Treasurer and let the closing agent settle it out of your proceeds. Selling ahead of the county's foreclosure auction keeps the choice of buyer with you.

How does a sale change the Detroit tax bill?

The buyer's taxable value is reset for the next year to the SEV, the figure the assessor sets at half of market value. The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor inside 45 days.

Must I repair my Detroit house before selling?

Buyers and their lenders often ask for repairs, and the contract decides who pays. Ask the City of Detroit about any compliance rules that apply to your property type, especially a rental.

How many people live in Detroit, and what do homes sell for?

Federal estimates for 2025 count 649,095 residents. For 2020 to 2024 the middle price tag on an owned house is $83,900, and about one home in two has its owner living inside.

What sets the pace of a house sale in Grand Rapids?

Pace here follows the neighborhood, the condition of the house and whether a landlord or an owner-occupant holds title. Grand Rapids is the Kent County seat and Michigan's second most populated municipality, with 198,917 residents in 2020 and an estimated 201,183 in 2025. As the economic center of West Michigan, it draws on a metro area of about 1.2 million people.

An owner can hire an agent, sell directly to another party, or accept a cash purchase of the house as it stands. The sections below tie each path to the city's rules, neighborhoods and numbers.

What shapes the Grand Rapids housing market?

Grand Rapids grew along the Grand River, at the rapids that stopped river traffic, and incorporated as a village in 1838 and a city in 1850. It earned the name Furniture City from its furniture makers, and office furniture companies including Steelcase and Haworth are still based in or around the city. Corewell Health is the region's largest employer, with its hospitals and research institutions along the Medical Mile.

The 2024 metro employer list also names Trinity Health, Gordon Food Service, Meijer, Gentex, MillerKnoll, Perrigo, Grand Valley State University and Grand Rapids Public Schools. A deep mix of health care, food, manufacturing and education jobs supports steady housing demand, and the Census Bureau reports that the city's population grew 1.2% from April 2020 to July 2025.

Quality-of-life draws add to the pull. The city hosts the ArtPrize competition, the Grand Rapids Art Museum, the Public Museum and Frederik Meijer Gardens and Sculpture Park, and its craft breweries, Founders among them, earned it the nickname Beer City USA. Gerald R. Ford International Airport serves the region.

  • The Medical Mile brings Corewell Health, the Van Andel Research Institute and Michigan State University's medical school together near downtown.
  • Grand Valley State University's Cook-DeVos Center for Health Sciences and Ferris State's College of Pharmacy sit on the same corridor.
  • Office furniture makers still anchor manufacturing in and around the city.

What do Grand Rapids homes cost, and who lives in them?

Owners and renters split almost evenly, and the middle owner-occupied home is valued at $244,500.

Numbers are from Census QuickFacts.

The 19-minute average trip to work is worth mentioning when you describe the house, since the Medical Mile, downtown and the freeways are all close.

Which Grand Rapids neighborhoods and roads do buyers ask about?

The city lists 37 distinct neighborhoods, among them Heritage Hill, Eastown, East Hills, Alger Heights, Creston, Garfield Park, Midtown, Belknap Lookout, Roosevelt Park and the North End. Mailing addresses are divided into NE, NW, SE and SW quadrants, with Fulton Street as the north-south dividing line and Division Avenue as the east-west one, so check the quadrant in any address you quote.

Highways shape commute choices. I-96 runs along the north and northeast sides, I-196 crosses east to west, US 131 runs north to south, and M-6 loops the south side. The Rapid operates the buses, including the SilverLine bus rapid transit route that opened in 2014, and DASH shuttles are free downtown.

How does Grand Rapids regulate rental houses before a sale?

The city requires a Certificate of Compliance before anyone lives in a rental unit. Owners register rental properties every year, and registration is free. Vacant properties must be registered within 15 days of becoming vacant. Certificates run two, four or six years depending on the property, and the city sends a reminder 90 days before recertification.

A rental inspection can end three ways. With no violations, the owner receives a certificate. With minor violations, the inspector gives verbal orders with a 14-day repair deadline. With major violations, a Notice of Violation sets a deadline of 60 or 120 days. Tenants should get 48 hours of notice before an inspection. Call Code Compliance at 616-456-3053 to check an address.

  • A landlord with a certified rental can hand the buyer a clean compliance record.
  • A rental that is vacant needs a vacant-property registration.
  • Rentals that use fuel-burning equipment must pass a mechanical safety inspection as part of certification.

Do Grand Rapids short-term rental and accessory unit rules matter?

They can if the property has a second unit. The city's zoning ordinance allows accessory dwelling units on single and two-family lots, and a June 2026 update allows an accessory unit of up to 1,000 square feet that is never larger than the main house. An accessory unit cannot be rented for fewer than 30 days, so Airbnb and Vrbo style use is not allowed, and a leased unit must be registered and certified as a rental. A deed restriction must be recorded so the unit is not conveyed separately from the house.

If your property has a second unit or a rented room, ask the Planning Department at planning@grcity.us before you list so the paperwork matches what you advertise.

How does Grand Rapids weather affect a house for sale?

Lake Michigan lies about 25 miles west, and the city averages 75.6 inches of snow a year, among the highest totals of any major American city. Lake-effect storms can arrive suddenly. Winters are cold and cloudy, summers are warm and humid, and the average growing season runs about 162 days, from a last spring frost near May 1 to a first fall frost near October 11.

Roofs, gutters, furnaces and basement moisture draw close attention from buyers in that climate. A seller who lists in winter should have the furnace serviced and the roof checked first.

What does the Michigan transfer tax cost on a Grand Rapids sale?

Michigan's county tax of 55 cents and state tax of $3.75 on each $500 of price are the seller's to pay (MCL 207.504 and 207.525), and the Kent County treasurer collects within 15 days after the deed is delivered (MCL 207.523).

At the city's median value of $244,500 that totals roughly $2,100, and the settlement statement will show the exact figure. The buyer notifies the assessor within 45 days so taxable value can reset to the state equalized value the next calendar year (MCL 211.27a), and a higher bill for the buyer is a common talking point in negotiation.

When does an as-is sale beat a listing in Grand Rapids?

Strong buyer demand favors a traditional listing for a house in good repair. An as-is sale fits deferred maintenance, an estate, tenant trouble or a firm moving date.

  • A listing fits an updated house when you can allow time for showings and financing.
  • An as-is buyer fits a vacant house, one with open code orders, or one that needs work before a lender would approve a loan.
  • Another landlord may pay a premium for a property that already holds a current Certificate of Compliance.

Ask for proof of funds, weigh offers by net proceeds, and put the closing date in writing.

More questions about Grand Rapids, MI

Does a rented Grand Rapids house need a compliance certificate?

Yes. The city requires a Certificate of Compliance before anyone lives in a rental unit, so a rented house should hold a current one. Call Code Compliance at 616-456-3053 to check an address.

Must I register an empty house in Grand Rapids?

Yes. Vacant properties must be registered within 15 days of becoming vacant, and registration is free. You can register online, by mail or at the Code Compliance office on Monroe Avenue NW.

Is an accessory unit allowed as a short-term rental?

No. The city bars accessory units from rentals under 30 days, and a leased unit must be registered and certified through Code Compliance.

What would Michigan transfer tax come to on a $244,500 Grand Rapids sale?

Roughly $2,100, from 55 cents per $500 for the county plus $3.75 per $500 for the state. The seller owes it, and the settlement statement lists the exact amount.

Will a Grand Rapids buyer pay more in property tax than I do?

Usually. Taxable value resets to the state equalized value in the calendar year after the transfer, and the buyer must notify the assessor within 45 days.

What is different about selling a house in Lansing?

As Michigan's capital, Lansing straddles three counties. Most parcels are in Ingham, some are in Eaton to the west, and some in Clinton to the north, which decides where your deed is recorded. Look at your tax bill first.

The July 2025 estimate is 113,884 residents, 1.1 percent more than the 2020 base. Homes here are valued well under Kentwood's or Livonia's, and only a little over half are owner-occupied, so a good share of sellers are landlords.

Lansing is also the center of a metro area of roughly 473,000 people, the third largest in Michigan. Michigan State University sits in neighboring East Lansing rather than in the city, and the Census counts 39.14 square miles of land inside Lansing itself. Some of that land, such as the airport tract, came under city control through temporary Michigan land-sharing agreements known as 425 agreements, which are not annexations under state law.

How did Lansing get its shape, and which neighborhoods matter to a seller?

Lansing was chosen as the capital in 1847 because it was more central and safer than Detroit, and it was incorporated as a city in 1859. Ransom Olds built Oldsmobile and later REO Motor Car here, and REO Town along Washington Avenue grew up around his factories.

The city is usually described in four sections, and buyers use the same names:

  • Eastside, east of the Grand River, centered on Michigan Avenue and the Frandor shopping center
  • Westside, around the river's curve, the most mixed by income and home type
  • Northwestside, the smallest section, near the Capital Region International Airport
  • Southside, the fourth section

Old Town, with buildings from the mid-1800s, and REO Town, along Washington Avenue, are the two historic districts people mention first. A listing that names its section and nearest corridor is easier for buyers to place.

Who buys houses in Lansing, and what keeps demand steady?

Government, education, insurance and health care keep Lansing's job base broad. A 2018 ranking by the Lansing Economic Area Partnership put the State of Michigan first with about 14,400 jobs, followed by Michigan State University, University of Michigan Health-Sparrow, General Motors, Lansing Community College, McLaren Greater Lansing and Auto-Owners Insurance. Jackson National Life and Delta Dental also appear on that list.

State and university payrolls mean steady renters and first-time buyers, and investors also look for small, older houses. If your house is a rental, expect investor interest first. If it is owner-occupied and updated, the broader market may pay more.

The school picture is mixed. Lansing School District covers most of the city, yet pieces fall into Holt, East Lansing, Okemos, Mason, Waverly, Grand Ledge and DeWitt, so confirm the district by address.

How easy is it to get around Lansing, and does that help a listing?

Lansing is crossed by I-96, I-69, I-496, US-127, M-43 along Saginaw Street and Grand River Avenue, and M-99 on Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard. Drivers reach Detroit or Grand Rapids in one highway run, which matters to buyers who commute or work for the state.

The Capital Area Transportation Authority runs 33 bus routes, and the Capital Region International Airport has scheduled flights and a UPS freight hub. A house within walking distance of a bus line or the river trail is worth naming in the listing text.

What does the Census say about Lansing housing and income?

The 2020 to 2024 Census figures show a lower-cost market than Kentwood or Livonia. They are the numbers an appraiser or investor will start from.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $128,700
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 53.8%
  • Median gross rent: $993
  • Households: 51,588, with 2.17 persons per household
  • Median household income: $54,382, and 20.1% of residents in poverty

At that price level, one big repair bill takes a large bite out of a sale. Get two contractor quotes on any big item before you decide between listing and selling as-is.

How does Lansing weather affect an older house?

Winters are cold and summers warm and humid. Snow arrives between early November and early April and averages 51.1 inches a season, and the temperature falls to 0 degrees Fahrenheit or lower on about ten nights a year. The city is largely spared the lake-effect snow that hits Grand Rapids.

For an older Lansing house, those numbers point to the usual trouble spots: aging boilers and furnaces, thin attic insulation, frost-damaged porches and wet basements. Buyers pay attention to these items in any inspection report, so a clear service record helps in either a listing or a cash negotiation.

Do Lansing landlords have to register rentals before selling?

Yes. Lansing requires every rental property to be registered with Code Compliance, with the exception of an owner-occupied single-family dwelling. The fee schedule effective July 1, 2024 lists a $235 new registration fee, a $55 per building fee for a change of owner, and a base inspection fee of $175 per building for one and two family structures.

When a rental is sold, the buyer takes on the registration, the inspection history and any open citations. Late fees and failure-to-register fees are listed on the same schedule, so an unregistered rental costs more to sell than a registered one. Ask Code Compliance for the current forms before you list a rental.

Vacant houses face a separate risk. The schedule includes administrative fees for red-tagged properties, emergency board-up and demolition, all of which can be assessed against the parcel.

What does the Lansing property tax calendar look like?

Lansing publishes a yearly assessment cycle, and its 2026 version shows the dates every owner should know. The same pattern repeats each year.

Lansing 2026 assessment cycle, City of Lansing Assessing Department
DateStep
February 14Last day to pay the prior year's winter taxes
February 20Assessment notices mailed
March 9 to 12March Board of Review hearings on valuation
June 1Deadline for a summer principal residence exemption
July 31Residential Michigan Tax Tribunal filing deadline
November 1Deadline for a winter principal residence exemption
December 31Tax day for the following year

The March hearing dates and the other 2026 entries are now in the past, but they fall in the same weeks every year. Ask the Lansing Treasurer when unpaid bills move to the county, because that date decides who you pay at closing.

What happens at closing and after a sale in Lansing?

Your deed goes to whichever of the three county recorders holds the parcel. The state tax on it is $3.75 per $500 of price, a county tax is added on top, and a handful of family transfers escape both. The title company can tell you which line applies.

Within 45 days of closing the buyer reports the sale to Lansing's assessor, and the house's taxable value is rebased for the following year. You, meanwhile, have 90 days after moving out to cancel your homestead school-tax exemption.

Weighing an investor's cash offer against a listing comes down to the net figure after taxes, recording costs and any city fees.

More questions about Lansing, MI

Which county records a deed for a Lansing house?

The county where the parcel sits records it. Lansing spans Ingham, Eaton and Clinton counties, so read the county on your tax bill and ask that county's register of deeds.

How much is the Lansing rental registration fee?

A new registration costs $235 and a change of owner costs $55 per building under the schedule effective July 1, 2024. Inspections start at a $175 base fee for one and two family buildings.

What is the median home value in Lansing?

Lansing's 2020 to 2024 median home value is $128,700, with median gross rent at $993.

When is the last day to pay Lansing winter taxes?

February 14 is the last day to pay winter taxes, per the city's assessment cycle. Ask the Lansing Treasurer when open bills move to the county.

Do I need to tell the city I sold my house?

The buyer reports the sale to the assessor, and you cancel your homestead exemption within 90 days of moving out.

Which Flint neighborhoods and landmarks matter to buyers?

Flint's neighborhoods are grouped around downtown, which is centered on Saginaw Street south of the river. Carriage Town and the Grand Traverse Street District hold preserved Victorian houses just west of downtown. East of I-475, Central Park and Fairfield Village sit between the University of Michigan-Flint and Mott Community College. East Village and the College Cultural Neighborhood on the east side are described as more stable, and the west side includes Mott Park and the Woodcroft Estates.

Public schools are run by Flint Community Schools, which operates ten elementary schools, one middle school and Flint Southwestern Academy. Catholic and charter schools also serve the city. Kettering University, UM-Flint and Mott Community College are all in or beside the city's core.

What are Flint's rental rules, and do they affect a sale?

They do if the house has tenants. Flint's rental ordinance requires rental properties to be registered with the city and certified after an inspection. A December 2023 city memo put the single-family registration at a one-time $250 and the inspection at $225 every three years, and it said tenants make up nearly half of Flint households. Landlords must provide heat from October 1 through March 31.

The same memo explains a water rule that surprises owners: the city prefers water accounts in the owner's name, and unpaid water bills become a lien that can be added to the property tax bill. Before selling a rental, make sure the water account is paid and call the Building and Safety Inspections Division at 810-766-7284 to learn where the certification stands. Fees change, so request the current schedule.

How does Genesee County tax foreclosure affect Flint sellers?

A delinquent tax bill can move a house into county tax foreclosure, and that is a real risk for owners of inherited or vacant property. The Genesee County Land Bank takes in properties through the tax foreclosure process: houses that go unsold at the public auction and are not claimed by the state or a local government are transferred from the County Treasurer to the Land Bank at the end of each calendar year.

Owners in the city can check parcel ownership through the city's property lookup, and a parcel listed under Genesee County LRC Inc or the Genesee County Treasurer is held by the Land Bank.   • Unpaid water bills can sit on the tax roll as well.
  • Ask the title company to pull liens early so surprises do not delay closing.

Two Michigan transfer taxes apply: 55 cents for the county plus $3.75 for the state on every $500 of price, per MCL 207.504 and 207.525. The seller bears them, and payment goes to the county treasurer within 15 days after the deed is delivered (MCL 207.523).

A sale at Flint's middle value of $53,500 would owe about $460, and the settlement statement will give the real figure. The buyer then notifies the city assessor within 45 days so that taxable value can reset the next year (MCL 211.27a).

When does an as-is sale beat a listing in Flint?

A sound house on a stable block can do well with an agent, provided the buyer's appraisal supports the contract price. When repairs would cost more than they add, or a lien, code order or tenant dispute clouds the deal, selling the house untouched removes most of the friction.

  • An agent listing suits a move-in-ready house when you can wait through loan approval.
  • An as-is buyer suits a house whose repair quotes outrun its likely sale price.
  • A neighbor suits an empty lot beside their home, a logic the Land Bank applies when it sells side lots.

Ask for proof of funds, read the closing date clause, and compare offers by what you keep after liens and costs.

Can unpaid property taxes be settled out of a Flint sale?

Usually yes, if closing happens before the county finishes foreclosure. The title agent subtracts the balance from your proceeds, and the Genesee County Treasurer can confirm the payoff and the foreclosure timeline.

Do unpaid Flint water bills follow the house?

They can. City rules let delinquent water charges become a lien added to the property tax bill, so a title agent will usually want the account paid before closing.

What does Flint expect of a landlord?

Rentals must be registered and certified after an inspection, repeated every three years, and landlords must supply heat from October 1 through March 31. Request the current fee schedule from Building and Safety Inspections.

What would Michigan transfer tax come to at Flint's typical home value?

About $460 on $53,500, combining 55 cents per $500 for the county with $3.75 per $500 for the state. Your settlement statement shows the exact amount.

What is the Genesee County Land Bank?

A county entity that receives tax-foreclosed properties that fail to sell at auction. It sells houses and lots, offers side lots to neighboring owners and demolishes dangerous structures as funding allows.

What is the Kalamazoo housing market like for a seller?

Kalamazoo is the biggest of these four cities and has the most renters. Mid-2025 estimates count 72,683 people, and just 42.3 percent of homes are lived in by their owners. Sellers here often hold a house near a campus, a former rental or a long-held family home, and the right route depends on which applies.

A listing, a private sale and a cash purchase all pass through the same city desks: the assessor, the treasurer and the rental inspection team. After those are settled, the deed goes to the Kalamazoo County Register of Deeds, which holds records dating to 1831.

How did Kalamazoo grow, and where do homes sit in the city?

Titus Bronson settled the site in 1829, and the town bore his name until 1836, when it was renamed for the river. Kalamazoo spans 25.11 square miles along a bend in the Kalamazoo River, with a flat northeastern section in the valley and low hills toward the west and south. Wikipedia counts 22 neighborhoods, many with a neighborhood association that works with the city's Neighborhood Development Division.

Kalamazoo sits midway between Detroit and Chicago on I-94 and lies 50 miles south of Grand Rapids. US 131, M-96 and M-343 tie it to nearby towns. The downtown Amtrak station anchors the 110 mph stretch of the Wolverine line between Porter, Indiana and Albion, Michigan. Flights use Kalamazoo/Battle Creek International Airport at the south end of the city. Weather runs hot and humid in summer with lake-effect snow in winter, and a major tornado crossed downtown in 1980.

Who lives in Kalamazoo homes?

Survey estimates for 2020 through 2024 describe a college town with mid-range prices:

  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $179,000.
  • Households: 29,523, with 2.25 persons each.
  • Typical rent: $1,078.
  • Adults 25 and older with a bachelor's degree or more: 38.5 percent.
  • Share of people at the same address a year earlier: 75.9 percent, the lowest of the four cities, which fits a place with many students and renters.

Estimates show a 1.2 percent dip from 2020 to 2025, so the market is steady. A buyer who plans to rent your house must register it with the city.

How does the Kalamazoo Promise figure into a sale?

Most of the city is served by Kalamazoo Public Schools, with small sections in Parchment, Comstock and Portage districts. Every resident graduate of Kalamazoo Public Schools has been eligible, since the class of 2006, for a scholarship covering up to 100 percent of tuition and mandatory fees for four years at any public university or community college in Michigan. The program is the Kalamazoo Promise, and buyers with children often ask about it.

The city also hosts Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo College (founded 1833), Kalamazoo Valley Community College and Davenport University, along with the WMU Homer Stryker School of Medicine, open since 2014. Houses near those campuses are more likely to have a rental history, which brings the city's rental rules into play.

Which Kalamazoo neighborhoods and employers shape buyer interest?

The city is commonly divided into 22 neighborhoods, and many have an association that works with the city on projects funded by programs such as Community Development Block Grants. Western Michigan University's West Campus, just west of downtown, holds the largest concentration of students, while Kalamazoo College sits on a hill opposite the university's original campus. Downtown centers on the Kalamazoo Mall, created in 1959 when part of Burdick Street closed to cars.

Local employers include Bell's Brewery, begun in 1985 as the Kalamazoo Brewing Company, and the A.M. Todd Company, a producer of peppermint oil and other flavorings headquartered in the city. Put the block, the walk to campus or downtown, and any association in your description, because buyers shop by neighborhood.

How does Kalamazoo's rental certification affect selling a rental?

The city requires registration and certification of every rental. After a passing inspection against the Housing Code (Chapter 17 of the city code), the owner receives a Certificate of Compliance. Inspectors may return at least every 28 months, and a courtesy notice arrives four months before expiry. Book the inspection about three months ahead and schedule any reinspection within 10 days.

Source: City of Kalamazoo Rental Registration Rules and Responsibilities. Give a buyer the certificate's expiration date and any open violations, and ask the rental inspections team to update the owner on the registration form after the sale.

What is the Kalamazoo tax calendar, and who can defer?

The summer bill is mailed by July 1 and due July 31, payable whole or in six monthly installments. Miss the first installment and the city adds a single 3 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest on the first of every month. The winter bill, mailed by December 1, is due February 14 in a single payment. After March 1, unpaid amounts are delinquent and go to the Kalamazoo County Treasurer.

A summer bill can be deferred to the winter date by owners whose household income last year did not exceed $40,000 and who fit one of these groups:

  • Age 62 or older, including an unmarried surviving spouse of someone who was 62 or older.
  • Blind, paraplegic, hemiplegic, quadriplegic, or totally and permanently disabled.
  • An eligible service member, veteran, widow or widower.

Applications reach the City Treasurer by September 15. Owner-occupants can also claim the principal residence exemption, which the city says trims a yearly bill by over 25 percent.

What exemption paperwork changes when I sell in Kalamazoo?

Sellers file a rescission of their principal residence exemption with the assessor, and a buyer who moves in files a new affidavit. Michigan also lets someone who buys a second home keep the exemption on the first for up to 3 years if it is empty, for sale, unleased and not used for business; the city's FAQ says that conditional form must be re-filed each December 31. If you use that option, confirm it with the City Assessor's office before listing.

What would a Kalamazoo deed cost in transfer tax?

Take the median value as a worked example. A $179,000 price is 358 units of $500. State tax is $3.75 a unit (MCL 207.525) and the county adds 55 cents a unit where it has under 2,000,000 residents (MCL 207.504), so the seller owes 358 times $4.30, or $1,539.40, to the county treasurer inside 15 days after delivering the deed. MCL 207.526 exempts gifts to a child or grandchild, court orders that state no price, and deeds that merely confirm existing title.

How often does Kalamazoo inspect a rental?

The city may inspect each rental every 28 months. Owners who renew on time and keep clean records can earn 40 or 52 month certificates with fewer visits.

When are Kalamazoo winter taxes due?

February 14, in one payment. The bill is mailed by December 1, and balances still open on March 1 are delinquent and payable to the Kalamazoo County Treasurer.

Can I defer my Kalamazoo summer tax bill?

Possibly. Household income last year must be at most $40,000, and you must be in a listed group such as 62 or older or disabled. Apply to the City Treasurer by September 15; the summer bill then falls due with the winter bill.

A scholarship for resident graduates of Kalamazoo Public Schools covering up to 100 percent of tuition and mandatory fees for four years at any Michigan public university or community college, starting with the class of 2006.

$1,539.40: 358 units of $500 at $3.75 for the state and $0.55 for the county, paid by the seller.

Interstates 96, 696 and 275 converge here, and M-5 adds another link, which is why a house near one of these roads is a short ride from much of metro Detroit (Wikipedia, Novi).

Novi Township was organized in 1832. Voters approved a city charter that became effective on February 24, 1969, drawing the city along the lines of the old village. Growth was quick through the later twentieth century, and Twelve Oaks Mall, opened in 1977, turned the Novi Road and I-96 corner into a regional shopping stop.

Most of the city drains to the Rouge River, and parts of the north and west sides drain toward the Huron River.   • Conditional rescission: someone who moved into a new Michigan home can keep a conditional rescission on the old one for up to three years, as long as it is listed, empty, unrented and unused for business.

City appraisers walk neighborhoods every year, and the State Tax Commission suggests that assessors inspect 20% of parcels annually, refreshing photos and sometimes measuring. They do, because buyers and their inspectors ask about work done to the house. Novi publishes separate applications for building, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work, and an owner acting as general contractor completes the Homeowner Permit Policy form.

The same page has an occupancy request form for new construction and warns that the Building Department needs two days' notice to process it. A temporary certificate of occupancy runs through the Administrative Board of Appeals. If you pulled permits for a kitchen, furnace, roof or addition, collect the final inspection sign-offs now. The Novi Building Department can supply a copy of any record you cannot locate.

What does the Oakland County deed office do after a Novi closing?

The transfer is recorded at the Oakland County Register of Deeds, reachable at 248-858-0597. Its fee page prices a deed recording at $30.00, a total that folds in a $4 state land-survey charge.

Any deed with a warranty covenant has to be tax certified at the Oakland County Treasurer's Office before recording, and the county lists a $5.00 certificate charge. The closing agent usually walks both steps over. Pages need a 2-1/2 inch blank strip at the top and a half inch elsewhere.

The county also posts its transfer tax: 55 cents for each $500 of consideration goes to the county and $3.75 for each $500 goes to the state. Look for both lines on your closing statement before you sign.

Within 45 days of the transfer, according to Novi's forms page. It goes to the city assessor, and your closing agent may be able to submit it for you.

Does the principal residence exemption stay with the house after a Novi sale?

No. The seller must rescind it with the assessor as soon as the home is sold, rented or left, and late filing triggers penalties and interest back to that date. A conditional rescission can last up to three years on a vacant, listed, unrented former home.

Which office takes the deed after a Novi closing?

The Oakland County Register of Deeds, not the city. Recording costs $30.00, and a warranty deed first needs a $5.00 treasurer's tax certificate, so most sellers leave the filing to their closing agent.

The record low is minus 22 F. Long stretches below freezing strain pipes in an empty house, the roof and the furnace, so a vacant property should keep its heat on through winter and have the roof and gutters checked before showings.

Which roads, schools and transit connect Pontiac?

Woodward Avenue (M-1) runs through town and loops around downtown, Huron Street is M-59, and Telegraph Road is US 24. I-75 and its business loop pass through. Amtrak's Wolverine connects Pontiac with Chicago through Detroit, three trips each way daily. SMART buses serve the area, and Oakland County International Airport is just over the line in Waterford Township.

The School District of the City of Pontiac runs Pontiac High School. Four charter schools operate in the city: Pontiac Academy for Excellence, Arts and Technology Academy, Walton Charter and Great Lakes Academy. Notre Dame Preparatory, a private Catholic high school, is in the northeast part. Buyers ask which one serves the address, so confirm with the district before you list.

Do zoning and historic-district rules touch a Pontiac sale?

They can. The city's planning forms include Zoning Board of Appeals applications, a Historic District Approval application and a Zoning Compliance application. A house in the Fairgrove Avenue district or another historic area may need approval for exterior changes, so a buyer planning work will ask what is allowed.

Curb cuts and driveways on state roads such as Woodward and Telegraph need a permit from the State of Michigan, not the city. If your lot touches one of them and you changed the driveway, keep the paperwork. Oakland County's Water Resources Commission runs soil erosion control inside Pontiac, which matters for a vacant lot or a house with grading work underway. For anything else, ask Pontiac planning staff what applies to the parcel.

Does Pontiac regulate rental houses that are being sold?

Yes. The city code requires owners of one- and two-family dwellings occupied by someone other than the owner to register them with the Department of Building Safety. A new owner re-registers within 60 days after a change of ownership, and late registration draws a $25.00 fee per rental unit per month.

  • Registered dwellings are inspected at intervals of no more than three years.
  • A vacated unit needs an inspection before anyone moves back in, and the owner must tell Building Safety first.
  • Occupying a unit before a certificate of compliance is issued is a municipal civil infraction carrying a $500.00 fine, with each day a separate offense.
  • A property whose recorded land contract names the occupant is exempt from the registry.

If you own a tenant-occupied house in the city, ask Building Safety for the certificate status before you sell. A buyer who plans to rent it will have to register within 60 days.

What does the Oakland County deed office handle for a Pontiac sale?

Recording belongs to the county, not the city. Staff examine each document and record those that meet statutory requirements.

Transfer tax applies when the consideration exceeds $99.99, and warranty deeds need a treasurer's tax certificate. The same office collects redemption payments on Sheriff Deed and Clerk Deed foreclosures, open only to people with an interest in the property, so an owner facing a foreclosure sale should ask about the payoff amount before picking a buyer.

Recorded documents can be copied through the county, and its index reaches back to January 1, 1964. If you inherited the house, pull the recorded chain of title early so a missing document does not hold up closing.

The city lists a Request for Income Tax Compliance Clearance among its income tax forms. Ask the Pontiac income tax office whether that clearance applies to your sale.

Can a Pontiac house with tenants be sold?

Yes, but registration and inspection rules apply. Pontiac requires one- and two-family rentals to be registered with Building Safety and inspected at least every three years, and a buyer must re-register within 60 days of the ownership change.

What is the penalty for occupying a Pontiac rental before inspection?

The ordinance sets a $500.00 municipal civil infraction fine, and each day is a separate offense. The owner or agent must notify Building Safety before a vacated unit is reoccupied.

Which office files a deed for a Pontiac property?

The Oakland County Register of Deeds. A warranty deed needs a treasurer's tax certificate at a $5.00 fee first, and a deed recording costs $30.00.

Pontiac averages 36.0 inches of snow a year. Roof condition, gutters and a working furnace matter most, and an empty house needs steady heat so pipes do not freeze before the buyer's inspection.

The Census Bureau reports $121,700 for owner-occupied homes in 2020 to 2024. That is a citywide figure, so compare recent sales on your own block before accepting an offer.

Where does a Kentwood home sale begin?

Kentwood sits in Kent County on the southeast side of Grand Rapids, and a sale there follows Michigan's county recording rules plus a few city offices you will deal with directly. Kentwood's July 2025 population estimate is 54,776, which is 0.8 percent above the 2020 base.

Most sellers meet three questions early: what the house might fetch, what the city requires before title moves, and how the tax bill is split at closing. This page answers each with Kentwood's own figures and offices, so any route you choose starts from local facts.

How is Kentwood laid out, and what does that mean for a home sale?

Kentwood covers about 21 square miles of land and is bordered by Wyoming on the west, Grand Rapids and Grand Rapids Township to the north, Cascade Township to the east and Gaines Township to the south. It was incorporated in 1967 out of Paris Township, partly to stop neighboring cities from annexing more land, and it took its name from the Kentwood Public Schools.

Road access shapes how quickly buyers can reach a house. The main routes are:

  • I-96, which clips the northeast corner of the city
  • M-11 along 28th Street, a busy commercial strip
  • M-37 along East Beltline Avenue and Broadmoor Avenue
  • M-6, the southern bypass linking I-196 near Hudsonville with I-96 near the Gerald R. Ford International Airport

Two paths, the Paul Henry Rail Trail and the East-West Trail, run through town, and homes near them tend to be easy to describe in a listing. School boundaries matter too: Kentwood Public Schools serves most addresses, while Forest Hills Public Schools and Kelloggsville Public Schools cover parts of the city. Confirm the district for your street before pricing.

What do the Census numbers say about Kentwood housing?

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures describe a city where owners are the majority and median rent runs $1,260 a month. The table lists the figures that bear most on a sale.

About four in ten homes are rented, so many Kentwood sellers are landlords, and the next section covers the rental certificate that affects them. A median value is a midpoint for the whole city. It will not predict your street, so ask for sold comparables from the same school attendance area.

Does winter in Kentwood affect what buyers look for?

Yes, because Kentwood has a warm-summer continental climate with real cold. Mean daily highs in January sit near 30 degrees Fahrenheit and mean lows near 15, and the area gets roughly 34 inches of precipitation across a year, spread fairly evenly from month to month.

Inspectors in town spend their time on the furnace, attic insulation, roof and basement. If one of them is worn out, either repair it before listing or sell as-is at a price that reflects the work. An as-is cash sale hands that repair risk to the buyer. Whatever route you take, get the furnace serviced and keep the receipt, because heating questions come up first in almost every walkthrough.

Does a rental house in Kentwood need a certificate before it changes hands?

A rental dwelling in Kentwood must be registered and hold a valid certificate of compliance, and that certificate stays with the owner who earned it. Under the city's rental dwelling inspection ordinance, a certificate can pass to a buyer only if the sale closes within 90 days of the certificate being issued and the buyer tells the city within 30 days of the sale.

The details that matter to a landlord seller:

  • A six-year certificate does not transfer. If it moves to a new owner inside the 90-day window it reverts to a two-year certificate.
  • Failure by the buyer to notify the city results in suspension of the certificate, and a replacement is dated back to the sale with fees owed from that date.
  • An owner who lives in a condominium unit needs no registration or certification, but a condominium owned as a rental is treated as a single-family rental.
  • Certificates cannot be issued while the property has unpaid city bills.

Call the Inspections Department at 616-554-0700 before you sign a contract on a rental, so the certificate dates and any open violations are known in advance.

When are Kentwood property taxes due, and how do appeals work?

Kentwood mails summer bills in the first week of July, due August 20, and winter bills in the first week of December, due February 14. Unpaid balances move to the Kent County Treasurer on March 1, and a qualifying owner has until September 15 to file a summer deferment with the city.

The assessment side runs on a fixed yearly rhythm:

  • Change notices go out soon after February 1 and carry the appeal dates.
  • The Board of Review begins hearings on the Tuesday after the first Monday in March, by appointment.
  • A homeowner still unsatisfied after the board has until July 31 to petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal.
  • Occupants claim the school-tax exemption on a homestead by June 1 to cover the summer bill, or November 1 for winter.

Appeals cannot rest on a neighbor's lower tax bill. Michigan lets taxable value rise more slowly for long-term owners, so a recent buyer will usually pay more than an owner next door who has held the house for years.

What happens to the tax bill and the exemption after a Kentwood sale?

After the deed records, the buyer owes the Kentwood Assessor a property transfer affidavit within 45 days. Taxable value then resets to the state equalized value for the next tax year, so the buyer's first full bill may look nothing like yours.

As the seller, stop claiming your principal residence exemption by filing the rescission form with the city within 90 days of moving out. Owners who already bought a new Michigan home while the old one sits unsold can ask for a conditional rescission, which Kentwood says may run up to three tax years if the house is never rented. The state form is 4640.

Recording happens downtown in the County Administration Building, 300 Monroe Avenue NW. Two transfer taxes attach to the deed: the state levy of $3.75 per $500 of price, and a county levy that Michigan sets at 55 cents per $500 below 2,000,000 residents. Your title agent should show both on the settlement statement.

Should you list in Kentwood or take an investor's cash offer?

An investor's cash offer usually closes faster and carries fewer conditions, while a listing reaches more buyers but adds showings and lender timelines. Neither is free of cost, so compare net figures.

Before you sign anything, list your own requirements: a closing date, the mortgage payoff and a plan for tenants. Ask each buyer in writing who covers recording costs and whether open city violations stay with the house. The Assessor's online sales search shows qualified Kentwood sales, which helps you judge whether an offer sits near the neighborhood's range.

Census data for 2020 to 2024 gives a median owner-occupied value of $268,200 in Kentwood. It is a citywide midpoint only.

Who collects Kentwood property tax, and where do unpaid taxes go?

Kentwood's summer bill is due August 20 and its winter bill February 14. Whatever is still open on March 1 goes to the county.

What paperwork follows a Kentwood sale?

Mostly the buyer's paperwork: the transfer affidavit goes to the assessor. Your part is the rescission of your principal residence exemption, plus a rental certificate check with Inspections if you were a landlord.

Can I sell a Kentwood rental with tenants still living there?

Yes, but the rental certificate must be valid and the buyer must notify the city within 30 days of the sale for a transferred certificate to stay in force. Call Inspections at 616-554-0700 first.

Which county office records the deed for a Kentwood sale?

The Kent County Register of Deeds, downtown at 300 Monroe Avenue NW. Transfer tax is collected at that recording.

What makes selling a house in East Lansing different?

East Lansing is a college town built around Michigan State University, and its rental rules decide who can buy and use your house. The city requires a rental license for most non-owner-occupied homes, some neighborhoods bar new rentals, and many single-family houses carry deed restrictions against renting at all. Those facts change which buyers can pay full price.

The city sits in Ingham and Clinton counties, immediately east of Lansing. It was settled in 1847 and incorporated in 1907. The legislature approved a charter proposed under the name College Park but changed the name to East Lansing. MSU was founded in 1855 and moved onto what is now campus ground in 1857, and the city's first seven mayors were professors or college employees. East Lansing stayed a dry city until voters changed the charter in 1968.

Grand River Avenue, a boulevard that grew out of the old Lansing and Howell plank road, runs through downtown and separates the campus from the rest of the city together with Michigan Avenue.

How does East Lansing compare with nearby Michigan cities?

East Lansing has the priciest owned homes of the four cities profiled in this batch of pages and the smallest share of owner-occupants. It is also young, with a median age of 21.8 at the 2020 census, so houses change hands and tenants more often than in a suburb like Eastpointe.

Only 59.5 percent of residents had the same address a year earlier, against 92.3 percent in Eastpointe. With that much movement, an East Lansing listing often meets buyers who plan to rent it out or buy a first home near campus.

What rental rules affect the value of an East Lansing house?

If your buyer plans to rent the house, the license rules matter as much as the price. The city code lists exceptions where no license is needed, and a seller can help a buyer by knowing them.

  • Family of the owner may live in the house without a license, and two unrelated people count as a family.
  • An owner who is away temporarily may use a house-sitting form for up to two years in a five-year period, but a house that is for sale does not qualify.
  • A seller of a house or duplex may stay up to 90 days after closing under a rental agreement without a license.
  • An estate representative may occupy a house for up to two years from the owner's date of death if the owner lived there for the last year.

Putting a house in an LLC removes the owner-occupancy exception, because an LLC has no family members. A new rental license is not automatic. Some areas have a zoning overlay that prohibits new licenses or limits them to owner-occupied homes, and the city's own guidance says a new application takes a minimum of two months and more often three to four. A tenant cannot move in before the license is granted.

Which neighborhoods, schools and roads do East Lansing buyers ask about?

The city lists more than 25 neighborhoods, and many have associations that speak at council and commission meetings. One section is a designated Historic District, and landmark structures in older areas fall under the Historic Preservation Code. Several single-family neighborhoods within a mile of campus have used a petition process under a 2004 zoning ordinance to restrict or prohibit renting.

East Lansing Public Schools reaches most addresses and enrolls just over 3,400 students in six elementary schools, MacDonald Middle School and East Lansing High School. Portions of the city fall in the Lansing, Okemos, Haslett and Bath districts, so confirm the district on the deed address. About one fifth of the East Lansing district's students come from outside the city through Schools of Choice.

Getting around is straightforward, and the Census puts mean commute time at 16.2 minutes, the shortest in this four-city group.

  • Interstates 96, 69 and 496 and US 127 serve the area.
  • CATA buses connect the city with Lansing.
  • Amtrak runs the Blue Water service to Chicago from the Capital Area Multimodal Gateway on South Harrison Road.

How do East Lansing property taxes work at closing?

The city treasury bills both seasons. Summer taxes are levied July 1 and payable without penalty through August 31. Winter taxes are levied December 1 and payable without penalty through February 14 of the following year. Weekend and holiday due dates slide to the next business day, and late payments pick up a 3 percent penalty.

On March 1 each year the city sends unpaid real property taxes to the county, with added interest and penalty. For a payoff after that date, call the Ingham County Treasurer at (517) 676-7220 or the Clinton County Treasurer at (989) 224-5280, depending on where the parcel sits. The city's property tax office, at 410 Abbot Road, takes calls at (517) 319-6826.

Because the city spans two counties, the register of deeds and the county treasurer that apply to you depend on the parcel. Ask the East Lansing assessor which county holds your records before you order a title commitment.

What state costs apply when an East Lansing house sells?

East Lansing sellers owe Michigan's transfer tax, which is $3.75 on each $500 block at the state level (MCL 207.525) with a county layer added (MCL 207.504). Ask the deed office in Ingham or Clinton County for the current county rate. The county treasurer collects it, and the clock is 15 days from handing over the deed.

MCL 207.526 also exempts a quitclaim deed that fixes a flaw in title and an instrument that straightens a boundary line without payment. After closing, the buyer tells the assessor of the transfer within 45 days, and taxable value is reset the following year (MCL 211.27a). Ask the assessor how to rescind your principal residence exemption so the new owner's bill is correct.

What should an East Lansing owner compare before choosing a sale route?

A listing aimed at students and landlords depends on the rental license history of the house, so gather license paperwork and any deed restriction notices first. An owner-occupant buyer cares about school district lines and neighborhood overlay rules instead. A direct sale to an investor can work for a house that needs repairs or has a lapsed license, as long as the contract states who handles the license process.

More questions about East Lansing, MI

Is a rental license part of selling my East Lansing house?

No. Licensing applies to renting, so selling does not need one. A seller of a house or duplex may even stay up to 90 days after closing under a rental agreement without a license, which can help when you need time to move.

Will the next owner of my East Lansing house be allowed to rent it?

Maybe. Many single-family houses carry deed restrictions against renting, some neighborhoods have zoning overlays that bar new licenses, and a license application takes a minimum of two months. Buyers should call the city's Planning, Building and Housing department before closing.

What are the East Lansing tax deadlines?

What does a seller in Lincoln Park have to do that sellers in most Michigan cities do not?

A Lincoln Park seller needs a Certificate of Approval from the city's Building Department before the house can be transferred. The city's ordinance on inspection of residential dwellings prior to sale makes it unlawful to transfer a dwelling, or to act as a broker for the transfer, without a current certificate.

The rule shapes the timeline of every sale in the city, however you find your buyer. The rest of this page explains how the certificate works, then covers the city, its housing figures and the tax and recording steps that follow.

How does the Lincoln Park Certificate of Approval work?

The ordinance (Chapter 1488 of the city's codified ordinances) requires anyone about to transfer a dwelling to register with the Building Department so an inspection can be scheduled. The fee is set by City Council resolution, so ask the department for the current amount.

The main points of the chapter:

  • A Certificate of Approval is valid for one sale or transfer, and a new inspection is required each time the dwelling is sold again.
  • A dwelling includes the house and accessory uses such as garages, sheds, pools, gazebos and playhouses.
  • A buyer may take responsibility for correcting violations by signing a notarized affidavit filed with the Building Department. If the violations are not corrected within six months, occupancy may be prohibited.
  • Failing to obtain the certificate is a municipal civil infraction with a $500 fine.

Inspectors may enter the premises during normal business hours to inspect, and owners, agents and occupants must give access to every part of the property they control. The enforcing official can also order immediate action to remove a hazard. Clear access to the garage, sheds and any pool or gazebo before the inspection date, because accessory structures are part of what the ordinance covers.

A transfer means a sale, a land contract or the exercise of an option to purchase. Gifts, devises and lien foreclosures are outside the definition. Rentals follow a separate track, covered below.

How are the certificates for owner-occupied and rental houses different?

Lincoln Park uses different certificates for different situations, and sellers sometimes confuse them. The table summarizes the three named in the ordinance.

Certificate of ComplianceRental dwellings and rental unitsThree years, unless the property is sold first
Certificate of OccupancyApproved use or occupancy under the zoning ordinancesIssued by the Building Department

A rental that holds a current Certificate of Compliance is not treated as a dwelling for the Certificate of Approval rule, but a new inspection and a new Certificate of Compliance are required before a rental is sold or transferred. If you own a rental, schedule that inspection before you sign a contract.

What is Lincoln Park like, and who lives there?

Lincoln Park is a Downriver suburb of Detroit in Wayne County, about 11 miles southwest of downtown. With only 5.84 square miles of land and 6,896 people per square mile in 2020, it ranked second in Michigan for density, behind Hamtramck. By the July 2025 estimate the city has 38,529 residents, down 4.3 percent from the 2020 base.

Its neighbors are Detroit, Allen Park, Melvindale, Ecorse, Wyandotte and Southgate. The north and south branches of the Ecorse River run through town and join before leaving it. Council Point Park marks the 1763 meeting where Pontiac urged tribal leaders to join him against Fort Detroit.

The city was laid out in 1906 as part of Ecorse Township, became a village in 1921 and a city in 1925. It grew as a bedroom community for workers at the River Rouge Plant and other auto and steel works, and two shopping centers opened in 1955 and 1956. Lincoln Park Public Schools serves residents through Lincoln Park High School, Lincoln Park Middle School and seven elementary schools.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $131,000
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 68.8%, with 14,767 households
  • Median gross rent: $1,023
  • Median monthly owner costs: $1,169 with a mortgage, $530 without
  • Same house one year ago: 91.3%
  • Mean commute to work: 24.4 minutes
  • Persons per household: 2.66, the largest of the four cities in this group
  • Residents under 18: 25.5%, also the highest of the four

Those figures, together with a bachelor's degree rate of 11.5 percent and a poverty rate of 21.5 percent, show a price level where a five-figure repair matters a great deal to a net result. Price the house with the inspection list in hand, since a buyer will do the same.

When are Lincoln Park property taxes due?

The city treasurer collects only current-year taxes. Summer bills are mailed by the end of June and fall due August 20, with later installment dates for owners who pay in parts, and a 1 percent penalty applies on the 20th of each month to unpaid summer taxes. Winter bills are mailed around the end of November and are due in mid-February, with a 1 percent monthly penalty after that.

All unpaid taxes transfer to the Wayne County Treasurer on March 1. The processor adds 2.95 percent to online payments, and a duplicate bill costs $10 unless you print the record from the city site. Title companies, agents and landlords are told this in a notice on the city's tax page.

Business personal property is taxed through the same office. Anyone operating on December 31 owes the following year's entire billing cycle, under state law.

How are a Lincoln Park deed and transfer tax handled?

Lincoln Park deeds are recorded by the Wayne County Register of Deeds. The Wayne County Treasurer must certify taxes on a deed first in most cases, and visits are by appointment. The fee schedule that began January 1, 2026 sets a deed at $26, with a $4 survey fee where it applies.

The state tax comes to $3.75 per $500 of price, with a separate county tax. State law exempts some conveyances, for example a deed given in foreclosure and a land contract that has not yet passed title, so ask the title company whether yours qualifies.

Afterward, the buyer sends the assessor a transfer affidavit within 45 days, and your own homestead exemption should be cancelled within 90 days of your move.

Do I need an inspection to sell my house in Lincoln Park?

Yes. Lincoln Park requires a Certificate of Approval from the Building Department before a dwelling is transferred, and a new one for every sale. Register with the department so it can schedule the inspection, and ask what the council-set fee is.

What is the fine for selling without a Certificate of Approval?

The ordinance sets the fine for failing to obtain a Certificate of Approval at $500, as a municipal civil infraction. It also states that other statutory and common-law rights and actions are not limited by that penalty, so a buyer or the city may have further remedies.

Can a buyer take over the violations in Lincoln Park?

Yes, by signing a notarized affidavit that states the buyer's intent to correct them and filing it with the Building Department. If the violations are not corrected within six months, occupancy may be prohibited, so a buyer needs a realistic repair budget and schedule.

Lincoln Park's median owner-occupied home value is $131,000 for 2020 to 2024, and median gross rent is $1,023.

When do unpaid Lincoln Park taxes go to the county?

Come March 1, everything unpaid belongs to the county treasurer, and the city no longer takes those payments.

Why does Holland's county line matter to a seller?

Holland straddles a county line, and that touches nearly every step. Thirty-second Street divides the city between Ottawa County on the north and Allegan County on the south, so the deed, the treasurer and the school district can all depend on which side your house stands. Whether the house is listed, sold privately or bought for cash, first confirm which county holds your parcel.

The city sits beside Lake Macatawa, about 5 miles east of Lake Michigan, and its 17.45 square miles split into 9.08 on the Ottawa side and 8.13 on the Allegan side. It is the biggest city in each county. Estimates for mid-2025 put the population at 35,372, up 2.9 percent from the 2020 base, the only one of the four cities in this batch that grew.

What is the Holland housing market built on?

Dutch Calvinist settlers under Albertus van Raalte arrived in 1847, and Holland received its city charter in 1867. A fire on October 8 to 10, 1871 burned most of downtown, which is why older homes gather in the Historic District and around it. Neighborhoods people mention include Holland Heights, Westside, Washington Square, Hope, Maplewood, South End and Downtown.

Jobs come from manufacturing, tourism, agriculture and higher education. Employers listed for the area include Herman Miller, Haworth, Adient, Magna and Kraft Heinz, with Hope College and a Grand Valley State University campus in town. The Tulip Time festival each May brings visitors who book local homes, so the short-term rental rules below include a festival category.

Where do Holland prices and ownership rates stand?

Holland leads Hamtramck, Jackson and Kalamazoo on home value. Survey estimates for 2020 through 2024:

  • Typical owner-occupied home: $252,200.
  • Homeownership: 67.8 percent of 12,977 households.
  • Typical rent: $1,193.
  • Persons per household: 2.34, and 23.6 percent of residents are Hispanic or Latino.
  • Average trip to work: 16.8 minutes.

Short commutes and a mix of furniture and automotive employers support demand, yet a house needing a roof, furnace or foundation work still sells below the typical price. A cash buyer pricing a repair-heavy house starts from the repaired value and subtracts the work.

Which offices and schools serve my Holland house?

Nearly all of the Ottawa County side lies inside Holland Public Schools. On the Allegan side, Holland Public Schools covers most of the area and Hamilton Community Schools the remainder. The city's own millage table reflects this with a separate Hamilton line.

Each deed goes to the register of deeds for its own county. Ottawa County records at its office on Fillmore Street in West Olive and offers a web portal for one-off e-recording, while Allegan County's register handles the southern side. Overdue taxes are a county matter, handled by the Ottawa or Allegan treasurer; the current bill itself comes from the city treasurer.

What does a Holland tax bill include, and what is the deadline?

The city dates the summer bill July 1 and sets the payment deadline in mid-August; the 2026 summer bill was due August 17. The winter bill follows on December 1. The city adds a 1 percent administration fee to both bills. Qualifying seniors and disabled homestead owners may ask to defer the summer payment; a 2026 deferral moved the due date to February 16, 2027.

Source: City of Holland tax estimator page. The 18-mill gap between the two columns is the school operating tax that a homeowner's exemption removes, so an investor who will not occupy the home pays the higher rate.

Can a buyer or tenant use my Holland house as a rental?

Chapter 14 of Holland's ordinance code governs rentals, which matters if tenants live in the house you are selling. Each unit must be registered, and the annual fee carries a December 10 deadline. An unregistered rental or unreported change draws a $200 late fee, and an unpaid annual fee is a misdemeanor. Inspections come every 3 or 6 years, the guide for monthly or annual leases lists a 3-year cycle, and a passing unit earns a Certificate of Compliance.

Short-term stays follow a separate track, and the city sorts them into three types:

  • Owner-occupied: your own primary residence, permitted in every zone.
  • Investor-owned: a home the owner does not live in. Permitted in mixed-use, industrial and similar districts; in residential districts, only within a cap of 25 properties and a 500-foot spacing rule. Ask the city whether any slots remain.
  • Tulip Time: a home offered no more than 10 days during the May festival, with no inspection or certificate required.

A buyer planning an investor-owned short-term rental in a residential zone should confirm capacity with the city first.

How is transfer tax figured on a Holland sale?

Sellers pay it. Michigan's state rate is $3.75 per $500 of price (MCL 207.525), and a county with under 2,000,000 residents adds 55 cents per $500 (MCL 207.504). A $250,000 price equals 500 units at $4.30, which is $2,150, payable to the county treasurer inside 15 days after the deed is delivered.

MCL 207.526 exempts gifts to a child or grandchild, court-ordered transfers with no set price, and deeds from foreclosed government-backed loans. If your lot touches 32nd Street, ask the register in each county how the parcel is recorded.

Which Holland tax exemptions end or start when the house sells?

Your principal residence exemption changes at closing. State law (MCL 211.7cc) has the owner file a rescission no later than 90 days after the house stops serving as a principal residence. A newcomer who moves in files an affidavit; the deadline is June 1 for the summer levy and November 1 for the winter levy. Holland's assessing office handles both forms.

Holland's tax page names other relief as well: a home repair exemption under Public Act 25 of 1978 that holds assessed value steady up to the sale, a poverty exemption (MCL 211.7u), and relief for disabled veterans. If you used any of them, tell the buyer, because the first bill after closing may look different.

How do the lake and climate affect a Holland house?

Lake Michigan tempers Holland's climate, which is classed as humid continental. January daily highs average 31.8 degrees with lows near 19.9, and an all-time low of minus 24 shows that a furnace failure in the winter can freeze pipes. Summer highs average 81.7 degrees in July. Homes near Lake Macatawa and the Macatawa River sit at about 610 feet of elevation, so expect your buyer's inspector to check basements for moisture, and fix gutters or grading before showings.

More questions about Holland, MI

In which county is my Holland deed recorded?

The one that holds your parcel. Holland spans Ottawa County (north) and Allegan County (south) with 32nd Street as the boundary, and each keeps its own register of deeds.

When is the City of Holland summer tax due?

Mid-August. The 2026 summer bill was dated July 1 and fell due August 17. A 1 percent administration fee is added to the summer and winter bills.

What happens to my Holland rental registration when I sell?

Registration and certification belong to the rental operation, and the city wants ownership changes reported. A missed report costs a $200 late fee, so tell the city about the sale.

Can my buyer operate a short-term rental in Holland?

Owner-occupied ones are allowed in every zone. Investor-owned ones in residential districts are limited to 25 properties with 500 feet of spacing, so check capacity first.

What is the transfer tax on a $200,000 Holland sale?

$1,720: 400 units of $500 at $3.75 for the state and $0.55 for the county. Family transfers to a child or grandchild are exempt.

What should an Eastpointe homeowner know before selling?

Eastpointe is a small, dense Macomb County city of 5.16 square miles, and most of what sellers deal with is rental registration, tax billing and school boundaries rather than a pre-sale inspection. Owners live in about seven of every ten homes, so many buyers are families looking for a first or second home.

The community was first settled by Irish and German immigrants in the 1830s. A post office opened in October 1897 under the name Half-way, because the spot sat near the halfway point of the stage run between downtown Detroit and the county seat at Mount Clemens. It became the village of Halfway in 1924 and the city of East Detroit in 1929. Voters approved the name Eastpointe in a 1992 referendum, partly to separate the city's identity from Detroit and to echo the nearby Grosse Pointes.

Downtown Detroit is ten miles southwest of Eastpointe. Warren lies to the west, Roseville to the north and St. Clair Shores to the east, and 8 Mile Road forms the southern edge beside Detroit and Harper Woods.

How does Eastpointe housing look in the Census figures?

The city peaked at 45,920 residents in 1970, slipped to 32,442 by 2010 and has hovered near 34,000 since. The rows below give the Census Bureau's latest local figures.
